parole.significato: -er, more (still used in compound verb-forming suffixes)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *-mp. In the Proto-Hungarian period it became -b due to regular phonetic change, then later lengthened to -bb. Cognates include Finnish -mpi.

parole.significato: -er, more (added to adjectives and certain adverbs to form the comparative)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *-mpa. Cognates include Finnish -mpi.

parole.significato: Originally, it was probably a diminutive suffix. In this sense, it is no longer productive. It can be found in place na…
parole.testo: It can be traced back to Proto-Finno-Ugric *-nt.
* From e (“this”). * From Proto-Finno-Ugric *-ë (interrogative particle).

parole.significato: Added to a stem - often an onomatopoeia - to form a verb expressing a (quickly) repeating or continuous action.
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *-ŋk.

parole.significato: Added to a word to express smallness, youth, unimportance, or endearment. When added to present participles, it can als…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric. Compare Finnish -kka and Northern Mansi -кве (-kve).

parole.significato: Added to a word to express smallness, youth, unimportance, or endearment. When added to present participles, it can als…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric. Compare Finnish -kka and Estonian -ke.

parole.significato: It is of ancient origin answering the question from where? It is no longer productive and is no longer an independent s…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *-lᴕ/*-lᴕ̈ place name suffix. Cognate with Northern Mansi -л (-l, ablative marker).

parole.significato: to worry about something, to be anxious about something or for somebody (-ért)
parole.testo: From the obsolete verb aggik (“to care about something”) + -ódik (reflexive or passive verb-forming suffix), where the verb is of disputed origin: either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *aŋke (“tight, depressed, distress, become tight”), or with a semantic blend and split related to agg (“very old”). A conne

parole.significato: brain (control center of the central nervous system), (in compounds) cerebral (of or relating to the brain)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ajŋe (“brain”), cognate to Finnish aivot and Estonian aju. Earlier compared with e.g. Finnish otsa (“forehead”), Komi-Zyrian водз (vodź, “fore, front”), Komi-Permyak одз (odź, “front part”) and derived from a suggested Finno-Ugric root *ońća, but most of these words are today
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ade- + -ik.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šoppɜ- + -ad (frequentative verb-forming suffix). Cognate with Komi-Zyrian шупавны (šupavny, “to dry up”) and Udmurt шупаны (šupany, “to dry up, to absorb”).

parole.significato: to decrease, reduce, lessen (to bring down the size, quantity of something)
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *šoppɜ- (*šappɜ-) + -aszt (“causative verb-forming suffix”).

parole.significato: handspan, span (the distance between the outstretched tips of the little finger and thumb when used as a unit of measur…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *sorɜ-śɜ (“span”). First attested in c. 1405.

parole.significato: leaf litter (layer of fallen dry leaves on the ground)
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric stem as avul + -r (obsolete noun-forming suffix). For the -r ending, compare tompor, hunyor, sömör, fodor.

parole.significato: to inaugurate (to induct into office with a formal ceremony)
parole.testo: From the av- stem of the obsolete avik (“to be absorbed, penetrate”) + -at (causative suffix), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *soŋe- (“to enter”). Doublet of árt.
Uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *palɜ (“left”). Cognate with Udmurt паллян (palľan, “left”). First attested in 1086.

There are two theories regarding this word's origin: * from Proto-Finno-Ugric *perɜ (“mud, marsh”); compare Komi-Zyrian переб (pereb, “banks of a forest river, covered in moss”) and Udmurt пера (pera, “soft, black mud; damp, muddy place”) * borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slav
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *poŋka (“knot, knob, protuberance, unevenness”). Cognates include Estonian pung.

Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *puńa (“to wind up, twist”) + -l (frequentative suffix) + -ít (causative verb-forming suffix). Cognates include Northern Sami bodnját (“to be twisted, crooked”).
From a stem of uncertain origin, perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *puke- (“to climb, creep”) + -ik. Cognates include Estonian pugema (“to crawl”) and Livonian puggõ (“to creep, to crawl”).

From a stem of uncertain origin, perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *puke- (“to climb, creep”) + -ik. The original form was bú, then búik, finally the variants bújik and búvik after the hiatus was filled with j and v, respectively.
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćappa- (“to chop, to beat with a popping sound”). Compare Erzya цяпамс (ćapams, “to clap”). Perhaps ultimately of onomatopoeic origin.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćelke- (“sparkle”) + -g (noun-forming suffix). Related to csillog (“to sparkle, to glitter”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćᴕlkɜ- or *ćᴕ̈lkɜ- (“to shine, gleam”) + -og (frequentative suffix). Related to csillag (“star”).
Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćukkɜ-rɜ (“flock, crowd”) + -r (obsolete noun-forming suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćolme (“knot, bundle; to bind”). Cognates include Finnish solmu (“knot”), Estonian sõlm, and Northern Sami čuolbma.
First attested in 1321. From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćuppɜ (“vessel, little pot made of birch bark”) + -r (nominal-forming suffix).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćᴕ̈ppɜ (“pinch, fingertip; to pinch”). Alternatively, possibly from Proto-Turkic *čɨm- (“pinch”), compare Chuvash чӑбат (čăbat), Turkish çimdik, çimcik.

parole.significato: tip, point (the sharp end of a conical object)
parole.testo: Uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćuća (“point, peak”), in which case related to Erzya цёцяня (ćoćańa).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *toŋɜ- (*taŋɜ-) + -ad (frequentative suffix).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *tërka. Compare similar words for crane across Eurasia, including Proto-Turkic *turńa (“crane”) (whence Turkish turna), Korean 두루미 (durumi, “crane”), Japanese 鶴 (tsuru, “crane”), Mongolian тогоруу (togoruu, “crane”)).

parole.significato: fore, forepart (the front; mainly used in possessive forms, chiefly eleje, or compound words, see elő-)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ede (“fore”). Cognates include Finnish esi- and Estonian ees.

parole.significato: to descend (to pass from a higher to a lower place; to move downwards)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šärɜ- (“to come, get, reach; spread”) + -eszkedik (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: to let go of (to release from one's grasp)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šärɜ- (“to come, to get, to reach; to spread”) + -eszt (causative verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: to row, paddle (to propel a boat or other craft over water using oars)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ewä (“fin”) + -ez (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: to wring (to extract a liquid from something wet, especially cloth, by squeezing and twisting it) (with -ból/-ből)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pućɜ-rɜ- (“to wring out, crush out”). Cognates include Finnish pusertaa (“to squeeze”).
Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric. It was a variant of fiú (“boy; son”) in the Old Hungarian era and it was formed through a formal and functional split from it.

parole.significato: grouse (any of various game birds from the order Galliformes, in the family Phasianidae)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *paδ̕tɜ (“male of capercaillie; Tetrao urogallus”). Cognates include Erzya пово (povo) and Komi-Permyak байдӧг (bajdög).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pëkka- (“to split, crack, split open, burst”) + -ad (frequentative suffix). Cognates include Finnish pakahtua (“to burst”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pakka- (“to split, crack, split open, burst”) + -aszt (“causative suffix”). Cognates include Hungarian fakad, Finnish pakahtua (“to burst”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *puna (“hair”). Possibly a doublet of pina. Cognates include Northern Mansi пун (pun, “feather, fur, wool”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pośe, borrowed from an Indo-Iranian language.

parole.significato: pot (a flat-bottomed vessel used for cooking food)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pata. Cognates include Finnish pata. With the noun-forming suffix -ék.

parole.significato: swallow (small, migratory bird of the Hirundinidae family with long wings and a forked tail)
parole.testo: An onomatopoeia with an uncertain origin. Probably from the same stem as the verb fecseg (“to babble, chatter”). It's also possible that it's from Proto-Finno-Ugric *päčkɜ (“swallow”). Cognates include Finnish pääsky and Estonian pääsuke.
* From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pintä- (“to close, cover”) (also reconstructed as *pentɜ-). Cognate with Finnish pinne and Udmurt поди (poďi).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *päjɜ (“white”) + -r (obsolete nominal-forming suffix). Related to Lule Sami pǟju (“white”), pǟjuk (“white reindeer”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *päδ̕ɜ- (“to milk”) or Proto-Finno-Ugric *pije- (“to milk”). Likely related to Erzya педямс (peďams, “to milk”) and Proto-Finnic *piimä (“milk”).

parole.significato: to lie (to be in a horizontal position)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *päkkɜ- (“to sit”) + -szik.

parole.significato: cloud (a visible mass of water droplets suspended in the air)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pilwe. Cognates include Estonian pilv, Finnish pilvi and Erzya пель (peľ). The computing sense is a semantic loan from English cloud.
Ultimately from Proto-Finno-Ugric *pilwe. Cognates include Estonian pilv, Finnish pilvi and Erzya пель (peľ).

parole.significato: pine, fir (tree of the genus Pinus)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pᴕ̈nɜ (“spruce”). Cognate with Komi-Zyrian понӧль (ponöľ, “young fir, young pine”).
First attested in c. 1372. Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *pëčɜ- (“color; to color, paint”) + -t (causative suffix).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *pučɜ- (“to lessen, decrease”).
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as fúl (“to drown”) + -jt (causative suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pačke like Northern Mansi пось (posʹ), Finnish paska and Estonian pask. For the verb sense, see also fosik.

Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *poδ̕ɜ (“shaving, splinter; to split”). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian пельны (peľny, “to split, to cleave”), пельӧм (peľöm, “chip, sliver”) and Udmurt пильылыны (piľylyny, “to split, to cleave”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pele (“column, stang”). Cognates include Finnish pieli.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *perkɜ or *perkkɜ (“worm”).
A compound of fi (a variant of fiú) + er(j) (an otherwise unattested term). The second element is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *irkä (“man, son, boy”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *puwa- (“to suffocate, strangle”) + -l (frequentative suffix). Related to Erzya повамс (povams).

parole.significato: ear (organ of hearing in humans and animals)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *peljä. Compare Northern Mansi паль (palʹ, “ear”) (Sosva, Upper Lozva), Northern Khanty пӑԓ (păł) (Kazym), Komi-Zyrian пель (peľ), Udmurt пель (peľ), Erzya пиле (pile).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *pᴕ̈rɜ (“bundle, raceme, bunch”) + -t (noun-forming suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *pećɜ (“willow”) or Proto-Finno-Ugric *pesɜ (*pečɜ) (“willow”). Compare Komi-Zyrian пача (paća, “willow”) and Udmurt пучы (pućy, “bud; pussy willow”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *jowkkɜ (“flock, crowd”) + -r (nominal-forming suffix). In Hungarian, it was originally a noun, which became an adjective in adjective use. Has been in the past compared with Proto-Finnic *joukko (“flock, crowd”) (whence e.g. Finnish joukko), but this is now explained otherwis

parole.significato: on foot, afoot, by foot, by walking
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *jalka (“foot”), compare to Finnish jalka (“foot; leg”), Ter Sami jillˈke, Estonian jalg (“foot; leg”).

parole.significato: army (a larger group of soldiers trained and armed for war)
parole.testo: From Old Hungarian hodu, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kunta (“clan, kin, community”). Cognate with Finnish kunta.

parole.significato: onion (Allium cepa, a monocotyledonous plant used as vegetable and spice)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *koćmɜ (“a species of bulbous plant”) + -a (noun-forming suffix or perhaps diminutive suffix).
From a stem of debated origin + -ít (causative suffix): # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kaja- (“to throw”). Compare Erzya каямс (kajams). # A cognate of hagy.

parole.significato: on one's back (in a supine position)
parole.testo: Lexicalization of Proto-Finno-Ugric *konɜ (“facing backwards, at the back”) + -tt (locative suffix).

parole.significato: anger (a strong feeling of displeasure, hostility or antagonism towards someone or something)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kira (“anger”) + -g (noun-forming suffix).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *karɜ- (*korɜ-) (“to bite”) + -p (obsolete instantaneous suffix). Cognate with Udmurt куртчылыны (kurtćylyny, “to bite”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kurńa (“groove, furrow”) + -ó (participle suffix).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic + -ad (“frequentative suffix”). Compare Proto-Uralic *korpe- (“to burn, be burnt, be scorched”).

parole.significato: dimness (the state of being dim, poorly illuminated, almost dark)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kumɜ (“shady, dark”) + -ály.

parole.significato: hook (rod bent into a curved shape, especially for fishing)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *korɜ- (“to scrape off, scratch, rub”) + -g (noun-forming suffix).
Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kule-. Cognates include Finnish kulua (“to wear out, to get consumed”) and Komi-Zyrian гылавны (gylavny, “to fall, to drop, to collapse”).

parole.significato: fat, flab (the soft, loose flesh around a person's belly)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kuje (“fat”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kaĺwɜ (“cuticle, membrane, scales”). Cognates include Finnish kalvo.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kala- (“to fish with a net”). Cognates include Northern Mansi хӯлп (hūlp, “net”), Finnish kalin and Estonian kale.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kolme (“three”). Cognates include Finnish kolme, Estonian kolm, Northern Khanty хәԯум (həłum) and Northern Mansi хӯрум (hūrum).

parole.significato: house, building (closed structure with walls and a roof)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kota. Cognates include Estonian kodu, Finnish koti, Moksha куд (kud). Not related to Proto-Germanic *hūsą or any of its descendants.

parole.significato: shell (egg, nut), skin (apple, onion, potato), peel (orange, lemon), rind (melon), crust (bread), bark (tree)
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1395. From Proto-Finno-Ugric *koja (“bark, skin”). Cognates include Finnish koja (“bark”).

Probably a derivation from an otherwise unattested stem of unknown origin + -g (noun-forming suffix). Alternatively, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kupla (“to bubble”) + -g (noun-forming suffix). Compare also Finnish kupla and Eastern Mari куво̄л (kuvōl).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kumće. Cognates with Northern Khanty хөс (høs) and Northern Mansi хус (hus).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *jakka- (“to go, get to”) + -tat (causative suffix).

parole.significato: thing, thingy, whatsit (a placeholder denoting a vague thing, or something whose name is forgotten by the speaker)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *atɜ (“thing, object”). Originally izej with the -j noun-forming suffix. Cognates include Northern Mansi ут (ut), Udmurt ot, Finnish asia, Estonian asi.

parole.significato: to go, to move between places, whether on foot or by transportation
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *jorkɜ (“to turn, wind”). Cognates include Northern Sami jorrat (“to rotate, to spin, to circulate”) and Proto-Samoyedic *jürə- (“to get lost”).

Uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *jukta- (“to speak, tell a tale/story”) + -ék (noun-forming suffix). Cognates include Finnish juttu (“talk, chat”) and Erzya ёвтамс (jovtams, “to say, to tell”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kelke- (“to be necessary, need to, must, be obligatory”). Cognates include Komi-Permyak колӧ (kolö, “have to, it is necessary, must”), Eastern Mari кӱлаш (külaš, “to have to, to be necessary”) and Northern Sami galgat.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerä (“round, turning; turn, twist”). Cognates include Finnish kiero (“curved, bent, twisted, crooked”).

parole.significato: to look for; to seek; to search for
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerä (“round, turning; to turn, twist”) stem as kerek, kerít, kerül + -s (obsolete frequentative verb-forming suffix). For the -s suffix, compare olvas (“to read”). Cognates include Finnish kierä (“twisted”), kiero (“twisted”). For the change of meaning, compare kerg
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root *kerä (“round, turning; turn, twist”) as kerül and kerít + -ing (frequentative suffix).
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerä (“round, turning; turn, twist”) as kering and kerül + -ít (causative suffix).

parole.significato: to get (to somewhere, to a location or into a situation, with lative suffixes)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerä (“round, turning; turn, twist”) + -ül (frequentative-reflexive suffix). Compare Finnish kierä, kiero, kiertää.

parole.significato: bream, ide (several fishes of the genera Abramis and Leuciscus)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kećä (“a kind of fish”). Cognate with Northern Mansi [script needed] (kāsəw). Possibly a Wanderwort. Compare Ossetian кӕсаг (kæsag), Georgian ქაშაყი (kašaq̇i).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kixe-, originally a word referring to the flirtation/mating calls of birds and/or the incantation/calling out of a shaman. Compare Proto-Finnic *kiima (“rut”) and Proto-Samic *kikëtēk (“to lek”).

parole.significato: to ask (for), to make a request (the person having -tól/-től and the favor, -t/-ot/-at/-et/-öt, or the person having -t…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerjä- ~ *kerä- (“to request”). Cognates include Finnish kerjätä (“to beg”), Komi-Permyak корны (korny, “to beg”), Udmurt курыны (kuryny) and Northern Sami gearjidit (“to beg”).

From Old Hungarian kér (“bark”) + -g (noun-forming suffix), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *keri or *kerä. Cognates include Northern Sami garra (“shell, crust”), Erzya керь (keŕ), Eastern Mari кӱр (kür, “bark”) and Northern Mansi кэ̄р (kè̄r, “shell, bark, crust”).

Of debated origin: # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kerɜ- (“to burp”) + -ődzik (frequentative-reflexive suffix). Related to Northern Mansi кēральт (kēralʹt, “burp, belch”). # From a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kēb- (“to chew”). Compare Turkish gevmek (“to chew”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kᴕ̈ćᴈ (“willing, ready”). Related to Lule Sami gisjuk (“willing, eager to do something”) and Ume Sami gissjòhka (“willing, helpful, accommodating”).

parole.significato: jug, pitcher (large serving vessel with a handle)
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic *kičɜ or *küčɜ (“vessel made of birch bark”).. If so, related to Northern Mansi коссум (kossum, “a type of box made of birch bark, with handles”). However, compare Serbo-Croatian krčag (“jug, pitcher”)
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *küńä. Cognates include Finnish kyynärä, Estonian küünar, Erzya кенере (kenere), Udmurt гырпум (gyrpum) and Komi-Permyak гырддза (gyrddźa).
Back-formation from körül. The kör- stem is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kere (“circle, ring, hoop, tire”). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian кор (kor) and Udmurt кури (kuri).
Lexicalization of kör + -é (lative suffix), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kere (“circle, ring, hoop, tire”). Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.
Lexicalization of kör + -tt (locative suffix), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kere (“circle, ring, hoop, tire”).
Lexicalization of Proto-Finno-Ugric *kere (“circle, ring, hoop, tire”) + -l (ablative case suffix).

parole.significato: gout (an extremely painful inflammation of joints)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from a Proto-Finno-Ugric stem + -vény (“noun-forming suffix”).

parole.significato: whetstone (a piece of stone used for grinding and sharpening tools)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kȣ̈sɜ- (“to grind, sharpen”) of onomatopoeic origin + -r (obsolete frequentative suffix) + -ű (obsolete present-participle suffix). Over time, the participle became a noun. First attested in 1331.

parole.significato: to follow (to go or come after in physical space)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *kijɜ- or *küjɜ- (“to follow, pursue”), with -t (instantaneous suffix). Cognate with Northern Mansi коюӈкв (koûňkv, “to chase, to pursue, to follow, to track”). The social media sense is a semantic loan from English follow.

parole.significato: a gap in space or time between two other parts
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *küti.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lakka (“cover, roof, shelter”), compare Finnish lakka and Estonian lakk.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lewdä- (“to find”). Cognates include Finnish löytää and Estonian leidma.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *läppɜ (“roof, cover”). Cognate with Udmurt липыны (ľipyny, “covering, roof”) and Lule Sami liehpa/liehppa.

parole.significato: flour (powder obtained by grinding or milling cereal grains)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from a Proto-Finno-Ugric verb.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lońća (“soft”).

parole.significato: flame, flare (the visible part of fire)
parole.testo: Of debated origin: # Native word, an onomatopoeia. # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lomɜ (“warmth, flame”) + -g (noun-forming suffix).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lᴕńćɜ (“horsefly, fly”). Cognates include Udmurt лузь (luź). The original velar vowel of the first syllable may have become palatal as early as in Pre–Old Hungarian under the influence of the following palatal *ńć, compare hegy and hős.

parole.significato: soul (spirit of a person thought to consist of one's thoughts and personality)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lewle (“breath, soul”) + -k (diminutive suffix). Compare Finnish löyly (“spirit”, obsolete) and Hungarian lélegzik (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: to hang (followed by -ról/-ről or -n/-on/-en/-ön) (to be or remain suspended)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *loŋe- (“to throw, push away”) + -g (frequentative suffix). Related to archaic Finnish luoda (“to throw, to cast”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lükkä- (“to bump, shove, push”). Cognates include Finnish lykätä.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lunta, compare with Northern Mansi лунт (lunt), Finnish lintu, Estonian lind, and Ter Sami lonnˈt.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *lewe- (“to throw, shoot”). Cognates inlude Northern Mansi лыӈкве (lyňkve, “to throw, to shoot”), Erzya ледемс (ledems, “to shoot”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *müŋä (“rear, beyond”). For a similar semantic development, see Finnish cognate myös (“also, too”). Of the same origin as mögött, mögé, and mögül.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *moĺɜ.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mińel (“sky”). Related to Erzya менель (meneľ, “sky”).

parole.significato: far (at a distance from something; used with -tól/-től)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mećä (“edge, side of something”). Cognates include Estonian mets (“forest”) and Sami miehćse (“far”).
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric stem as messze.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *muja- (“to touch, feel”) + -tat (causative suffix). Cognates include Finnish muistaa (“to recall, remember”) and Estonian mõistma (“to understand”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mälke (“breast”). Its origins may be the same as the word mell (“breast”). For sense 3, a borrowing from Romanian mal (“river bank”) is also plausible.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mu. Cognates include Northern Mansi мо̄т (mōt, “other, second, foreign”) and Finnish muu.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mekše. Cognates include Finnish mehiläinen, Estonian mesilane, Erzya мекш (mekš).

Lexicalization of the dialectal noun mög (“space behind something”) + -é (locative suffix). The base word is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *miŋä or *müŋä (“space behind something”). Cognates include Finnish myös.

Lexicalization of the dialectal noun mög (“space behind something”) + -ött (locative suffix). The base word is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *miŋä (*müŋä) (“space behind something”). Cognates include Finnish myös and Erzya мей (mej, “reverse (side)”), мейле (mejle, “later”). From the same root as meg.
Lexicalization of the dialectal mög (“space behind something”) + -l (ablative suffix), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *miŋä (*müŋä) (“space behind something”).

parole.significato: to pass, to go by, to elapse
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mule-. Cognates include Moksha and Erzya молемс (molems, “to go”), Northern Sami mollat.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *nᴕńćɜ (“strong, hard”). Cognates include Komi-Permyak нач (nać, “entirely, totally”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic *anɜ (anɜppɜ) (“mother-in-law”); later also attested as nap (now obsolete; unrelated to Hungarian nap (“sun; day”)).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ne (“no, not”). In the Ob-Ugric languages, it has been used only in pronominal forms such as Northern Mansi нэ̄матыр (nè̄matyr, “nothing”), нэ̄мхо̄т (nè̄mhōt, “nowhere”), нэ̄мхуньт (nè̄mhunʹt, “never”) (Sosva) and Northern Khanty нємхуйат (nêmhujat, “nobody”) (Kazym) or нємәԓ

parole.significato: tongue (the fleshy muscular organ in the mouth of a mammal)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńälmä. Cognates include Northern Mansi не̄лум (nēlum, “tongue”) and Northern Sami njálbmi (“mouth”).
First attested in 1452. From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńëre.
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńuŋɜ- (“to rest, relax”) stem as nyugszik + -alom.

* From the second part of the compound word napnyugat ("sunset"). * From the same, now archaic Hungarian verb nyug (“to keep quiet”), the same word from which nyugszik and nyugodt derive. This in turn derives from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńuŋV (“to rest”).
From the same, now archaic Hungarian verb nyug (“to keep quiet”), the same word that nyugszik and nyugat derive from. This in turn derives from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńuŋV (“to rest”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńuŋɜ- (“to rest, relax”) + -szik. The nyug- (“to keep quiet”) stem was revived during the Hungarian language reform in the 18th–19th centuries and used in several compound words. See nyugágy (“deckchair”), nyugdíj (“pension”). Cognate with Erzya нувсемс (nuvsems, “to doze, dr

parole.significato: rest, peace (a state of tranquility and quiet)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńuŋɜ- (“to rest”), the same stem as that of nyugszik and nyugalom + -ta (noun-forming suffix amalgamated with the possessive).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńolke.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic *ńire- (“to scratch, scrape”)
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńüre.

parole.significato: to stretch, to extend, to lengthen, to prolong
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *nᴕjɜ- (ńᴕjɜ-) (“to stretch, extend”) + -jt (causative suffix). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian нёкравны (ńokravny, “to bend down, to bow, to curve”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *neljä. Cognates include Northern Mansi нила (nila), Finnish neljä, Estonian neli, Northern Sami njeallje, Northern Khanty няԯ (njał).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *näke-. Cognates include Finnish nähdä.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *omte; cognate with Finnish onsi (“hollow, space”) & ontelo (“cavity”) and Erzya ундо (undo, “hole, cavity”).
From a variant of the same Proto-Finno-Ugric stem as alszik (“to sleep”) + -t (causative suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *sula (“to molten, melted; melt, dissolve”) + -ad (frequentative-instantaneous suffix). Cognates include Northern Mansi толуӈкве (toluňkve) and Finnish sulaa.

parole.significato: to melt (to cause something to melt)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *sula (“to molten, melted; melt, dissolve”) + -aszt (“causative suffix”). Cognates include Finnish sulaa.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *arpa (“soothsaying instrument, magic instrument, potion”) + -os (noun-forming suffix indicating occupation). The Finno-Ugric words may have Turkish relations. Compare Ottoman Turkish آغری (ağrı, “pain, ache”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *oća or *ońća (“part; to part, share, divide”) + -lik (frequentative-reflexive suffix). Cognates include Finnish osa (“part”), Estonian osa (“part”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *oća or *ońća (“part; to part, share, divide”) + -t (causative suffix). Cognates include Finnish osa (“part”), Estonian osa (“part”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *puna (“hair”). Possibly a doublet of fan.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *rakkɜ- (“to make, prepare, build”). Cognates include Finnish rakentaa.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *reŋkɜ (“warm, heat, hotness”). Cognates include Northern Mansi ре̄г (rēg, “heat, warmth”) and Komi-Zyrian регыд (regyd, “soon, shortly”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *rakka (“near; to approach”). Cognates include Finnish rakas (“dear, beloved”).

parole.significato: cloth (a piece of cloth used for cleaning)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *raćɜ (“rag”). Possibly from Turkic, compare Old Turkic [script needed] (uruŋu), Proto-Slavic *xorǫgy, Mongolian оронго (orongo).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *roćɜ (“tired, weak, thin”). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian рудзавны (rudźavny, “to get tired, to be exhausted”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *räćɜ (“piece, part”).

parole.significato: to notch, carve, engrave, cut into, nick, score
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *rokɜ- (“to cut, chop up”). Cognates include Eastern Mari руаш (ruaš, “to cut, to chop”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; perhaps; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: ugly, hideous (displeasing to the eye; not aesthetically pleasing)
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *rᴕtɜ (“breakable, stiff, dry-rotten”).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *čaćkɜ (“a species of bird of prey”). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian сюзь (śuź).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *čappa + -ny (nominal-forming suffix) + -ú (adjective-forming suffix). Cognates include Finnish hapan and Estonian hapu. First attested in c. 1430.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śäŋkɜ (“buttocks”). Cognate with Northern Mansi са̄ӈкв (sāňkv, “waist, loins, small of the back”)

Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *čäŋkᴕ- (“to help”) + -ít (verb-forming suffix). For the first element, compare the чанго- (čango-) stem of Erzya чангодемс (čangodems, “to help, to have mercy”), with verb-forming suffix -д (-d), verb stem -е, and infinitive suffix -мс (-ms). For the correspondance b
Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *čijɜ- (“to run”) + -t (instantaneous verb-forming suffix). Related to Erzya чиемс (čijems).

parole.significato: thin, slim, slender (having little body fat or flesh)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šupa (“lean, thin”) + -ny.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćaδa- (“run, to run”) or perhaps from Proto-Uralic *śaδa- + -ad (“frequentative suffix”). See the same root in szalaszt and szalajt.

parole.significato: shit (solid excretory product evacuated from the bowel)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćara- (“excrement, shit”). Cognates include Northern Khanty щор (sjor, “excrement of animals or birds; dung, manure”).

parole.significato: horn (the hard substance from which animals' horns are made, sometimes used by man as a material for making various obj…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śarwe.

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śarwe. Cognates include Finnish sarvi, Estonian sarv. The Proto-Finno-Ugric term is in turn from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćr̥Hwás, compare Avestan 𐬯𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬁 (sruuā, “horn”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-; see there for more.

parole.significato: to take from somewhere, to collect
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *śentä- (“to tear down, rip, break off”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćäŋkɜ or *śäŋkɜ. Compare Proto-Finnic *sänki (“stubble”) and descendants.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śälä- (“to cut, cut up, slice”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śala (“elm”).

An obscured compound. The first half is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *śoma- (“hunger, thirst”). The second half is juh - internal organ, stomach. It may have originally been a noun meaning thirsty stomach. The noun developed into an adjective over time. Cognate to Udmurt сюмэм (śumem, “hungry”).
From *szomor + -ú (present participle suffix), from the same root as szomjas, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *śoma-.

parole.significato: to worry, be anxious, be tense, be in a state of angst
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śorɜ (“narrow”) + -ong (frequentative verb-forming suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćura (“ridge ?”) + -os (adjective-forming suffix). Uses the same root as szorít.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćura (“ridge ?”) + -ít.

parole.significato: gorge (a deep, narrow valley with steep sides, usually hollowed out by water)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śorɜ (“narrow”) + -dok (noun-forming suffix). The szur- stem is a variant of szor- found in the verbs szorít (“to press, grip, pinch, urge”), szorong (“to be crowded together, stressed, anxious”), etc.

parole.significato: pitch (dark, extremely viscous material made by distilling tar)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śure. Cognates include Komi-Permyak сир (śir) and Udmurt сир (śir).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śarɜ- (“to become dry”). Cognate with Northern Khanty сорты (sorty, “to dry”), сорәм (sorəm, “dry, dried out”), and Eastern Khanty сорта (sorta, “to dry”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śarɜ- (“dry; to become dry”) + -z (obsolete noun-forming suffix). Cognate with Northern Khanty сорты (sorty, “to dry”), сорәм (sorəm, “dry, dried out”), and Eastern Khanty сорта (sorta, “to dry”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śarɜ- (“to dry, become dry”) + -ít.

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śëta (“hundred”). Cognates include Northern Mansi са̄т (sāt, “hundred”), Finnish sata and Estonian sada. Originally borrowed from an Indo-Iranian language; compare Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬙𐬀 (sata), Sanskrit शत (śatá).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *selɜ (“edge”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śine (“charcoal”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćuγз or *śukз (“woodworm”).

parole.significato: to prick, to pierce, to stab (with a sharp tool, e.g. a needle or a knife; into some body part: -ba/-be or -n/-on/-en/-…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śurwa- (“to thrust, push”). Cognates include Finnish survoa and Estonian suruma.

parole.significato: grey (having a color somewhere between white and black, as the ash of an ember)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćerɜ (“grey”) + -ke (diminutive suffix).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śäŋe (“hair, plait of hair; braid; to braid”). Cognates include Northern Mansi сагуӈкве (saguňkve, “to weave”).

parole.significato: mantle or coat (the traditional long embroidered felt cloak of Hungarian shepherds)
parole.testo: Split from the Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćerɜ (“grey”) base word of the adjective szürke (“grey”).
Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *süćɜ. Cognate with Komi-Zyrian сӧдз (södź, “clear, pure”).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *čappɜ (“pail, faint”) + -ad (verb-forming suffix).
From the old Hungarian sérik (“to get hurt, to ache”) + -t (causative suffix). The verb sérik is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćärke- (“have pain, hurt”).

From Old Hungarian ſyher (šiɣer), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *čikere. First attested in 1055. According to the New Etymological Dictionary of Hungarian it is of uncertain origin and the Finno-Ugric origin is incorrect for chronological and phonological reasons.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *śijele. Cognates include Finnish siili and Estonian siil. Compare Hungarian sün (“hedgehog”).

parole.significato: hedgehog (a small mammal of the subfamily Erinaceinae)
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *śijele (“hedgehog”) as Finnish siili and Estonian siil. Compare Hungarian sül (“porcupine”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: To force someone or something to remain in place or in position by counteracting another force.
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *tarttɜ- (“to cling to, stick to, get caught”), compare Proto-Finnic *tarttudak (“to stick, adhere; grab, seize”).

Either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *towke (“spring”), with such cognates as Finnish touko, Komi-Zyrian тулыс (tulys), Udmurt тулыс (tulys), Northern Mansi тӯя (tūâ). Alternatively, related to Turkic forms such as Chuvash tu-, tăv- or Nogai tuv- ´to be born, to give birth´. Hungarian tavasz (tava- root +
First part from Proto-Finno-Ugric, te + hát

parole.significato: lot (US), parcel (of land), plot, piece of ground (an area or land used for building on or planting on)
parole.testo: The etymology is disputed. It has been derived in at least three ways: * From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as the verb telik (“to fill”). * From tel (“ground, soil”) + -k (noun suffix). For the same suffix, compare lélek (“soul”). * From Oghur *tilök “separated (area)”, from Proto-Turkic *til (“t
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *täwδe- or Proto-Uralic *täwde, (*tälkɜ-) (“complete, full”) + -ik (reflexive suffix).

parole.significato: to hang out / hang up (to dry)
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as terít + -eget.

parole.significato: to set (to arrange the table with dishes and cutlery)
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as tereget and terül + -ít (causative suffix).

parole.significato: to do (optionally with -val/-vel for the target person or object)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *teke-. Cognates include Finnish tehdä, Karelian tehtä and Estonian tegema.

parole.significato: corpse, cadaver, dead body (of a person)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *täktä (“bone, skeleton”) + -m (noun-forming suffix).

Of uncertain origin: * Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *tajwe (“area, place”), thus being related to Southern Sami dajve (“area”), but this dubious root is sparsely attested across the Uralic languages (only in Samic and Hungarian). * Possibly from Proto-Ugric *taɣɜ (“place”). Cognates include North

A lexicalized comparative form. From Proto-Finno-Ugric *teppɜ (“thick, tight”) + -b (comparative suffix). Related to Komi-Permyak топыт (topyt, “dense, compact, thickset”) and Udmurt тупыттэм (tupyttem, “too much”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *temɜ (“full, complete; stuff, fill”).

parole.significato: to dig (to move earth out of the way, especially downward to make a hole)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *tüŋe. Cognates include Estonian tüvi, Finnish tyvi, Eastern Mari тӱҥ (tüŋ), Komi-Zyrian дин (ďin).
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *terä (“cutting edge, peak, tip”), though ő is unexpected. Tálos (1993) proposes derivation from Proto-Iranian *tigra-, compare e.g. Persian تیر.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wamta (“forest”).

parole.significato: butter (a soft, fatty foodstuff made by churning the cream of milk (generally cow's milk))
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *waje. Cognates include Northern Mansi во̄й (vōj), Finnish voi and Estonian või.

From Old Hungarian vagyon. See Hungarian volt. * Forms beginning with v- are from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wole- (“to be”). Cognate with Northern Mansi о̄луӈкве (ōluňkve), Finnish olla and Estonian olema. Compare inflected forms such as volt, volna, való and Old Hungarian vola or vala. See also vagy for t

parole.significato: to sew (to use a needle to pass thread repeatedly through pieces of fabric in order to join them together)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *worka-. Cognates include Komi-Zyrian вурны (vurny) and Udmurt вурыны (vuryny).

parole.significato: marrow, bone marrow (the fatty vascular tissue that fills the cavities of bones)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wideme.
Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *waćɜ (“thin, bendable branch or twig”) + -ő (diminutive suffix). Cognates include Eastern Mari вазе (vaze, “bow”) and Northern Sami vážus (“lath, slat, bar”).
Uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wettä- (“to throw, fling, toss”). Compare Erzya видемс (videms, “to sow”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wića- (“see, look, watch”) -z (frequentative suffix). Cognates include Komi-Zyrian видзны (vidźny) and Udmurt возьыны (voźyny), возьманы (voźmany).

Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *walke (compare Finnish valkea, Estonian valge, and Northern Sami vielgat). Sense 1 is a semantic loan from Slavic, which displaced the original meaning illumination. Compare Romanian lume and Old Church Slavonic свѣтъ (světŭ). First attested in the 12th c. Doublet o
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as világ + -ad (frequentative-inceptive suffix).
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root as világ + -ul (frequentative-reflexive suffix). For the vir- stem compare virág (“flower”) and virrad (“to dawn”).

Inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *walke, with the semantic shift of light > radiance, sparkle > flower. For the semantic development, compare Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos). First attested in 1237. Doublet of világ.
From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *wole- or *woli- as Finnish and Estonian olla. Compare similarities with Old Hungarian vola, later vala (same meaning).

parole.significato: to become, to turn or turn into (something -vá/-vé or -ra/-re with valóra)
parole.testo: Most likely from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wëlka-. Cognate with Finnish valkama (“boat-shore, spot on the banks where a path across ice or water starts, haven”), Northern Sami vuolgit (“to go, leave, depart, be, become, go out from”), Eastern Mari волем (voĺem, “to go down, fall”), and Northern Mansi [scri
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wäntɜ- (“to see, look at, watch”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wiŋe. Cognate to Finnish viime and Estonian viimane.

parole.significato: thin, narrow (having a small diameter or thickness)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wekkɜ (“thin”) + -ny. Related to Udmurt векчи (vekći) and Komi-Zyrian векни (vekńi).
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wᴕ̈nɜ (“old”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wäŋćɜ (“knife; cut”). Cognates include Finnish veitsi.

parole.significato: plague, pestilence, pandemic, disease (today only in some compounds, especially referring to domestic animals)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wäsä- (“to pass by, disappear”) (whence also Northern Sami vássit (“to pass, disappear”)).

parole.significato: noise (various sounds, usually unwanted or unpleasant)
parole.testo: From the same Proto-Finno-Ugric root *śoje as Northern Mansi суй (suj, “noise”) and Finnish soida.

Of debated origin: * By semantic split from the above term, or *from the same Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćaka (“drift ice, thin ice”) (or *śaka) as Western Mansi [script needed] (sai̊) and Northern Sami [Term?] (čuokke -g̬-).

parole.significato: bed (a piece of furniture, usually flat and soft, on which to rest or sleep)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *aďo (“bed”) (whence also Proto-Permic *woľ, Proto-Samic *vuoδō and Proto-Finnic *voodëk), possibly derived from Proto-Finno-Ugric *aďe- (“to spread, make the bed”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ońća, with semantic shift "meat" > "thick meat" > "loins". Compare Southern Mansi [script needed] (ońćī, “buttocks”), with the word-final -k (nominal-forming suffix), compare fészek and lélek.

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *alɜ- (“to recite an incantation, cast a spell on, enchant”) + -d (frequentative suffix). Cognates include Erzya алтамс (altams, “to vow”) and Eastern Mari улдаш (uldaš, “to pray”). Possibly related to átkoz (“to curse, damn”); for the change of meaning, compare e.g. Latin sac
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ola. Compare Erzya уло (ulo, “chin”).

parole.significato: to stand (to be in an upright position)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *salkɜ- (“to stand”).

parole.significato: dream (imaginary events seen in the mind while sleeping)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *adema (“sleeping, dream”). Cognates include Erzya удома (udoma), Eastern Mari омо (omo) and Northern Mansi ӯлум (ūlum, “dream”).

parole.significato: awl (pointed instrument for piercing small holes, as in leather or wood)
parole.testo: From the Proto-Finno-Ugric *ora (“awl”).

parole.significato: to harm, hurt someone, to be bad or harmful to someone (with -nak/-nek)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *arja- (“to tear”).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *orpa (“orphan”). Cognates include Finnish orpo, Estonian orb and Erzya уроз (uroz), originally from an Indo-European language (Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos). Compare Sanskrit अर्भ (árbha), Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós), Armenian որբ (orb). Doublet of rab.  PIE word  *h₃ór

parole.significato: sky (the part of the atmosphere which can be seen above a specific place)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *säŋe. Cognates are limited to Baltic-Finnic (e.g. Finnish sää (“weather”)) and Komi-Permyak сынӧд (synöd, “warm air”).

parole.significato: to burn, to be on fire (to be consumed by fire, or in flames)
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Finno-Ugric *äŋɜ- (“fire; to burn”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *äne. Cognates include Estonian hääl, Finnish ääni.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ikä. Cognates include Finnish ikä, Estonian iga and Erzya ие (ije).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ikene. Cognate with Finnish ien and Estonian ige.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ećɜ (“younger brother or sister”). Cognates include Udmurt узьы (uźy, “sister-in-law”).
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wide- (“to kill”). Cognates include Northern Mansi алуӈкве (aluňkve) and Komi-Zyrian вины (viny).
From the ö- stem of a Proto-Finno-Ugric third-person singular pronoun (present-day ő), with the obsolete pronoun suffix -n.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wuďe. Cognates include Komi-Zyrian выль (vyľ), Eastern Mari у (u), Finnish uusi and Estonian uus.

parole.significato: master (someone who has control over something or someone)
parole.testo: Of debated origin: # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *urɜ (“man, male”). # Borrowed from a Turkic language before the times of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin (at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries), from Proto-Turkic *ūŕ (“master, craftsman”). Compare Karakhanid اُوزْ (ūz, “skillful”) and
Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *siδ̕ɜ (“hurry, endeavour; quick, zealous”).
Of debated origin: # A native word splitting from the archaic variant of víz (“water”). # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *siδ̕ɜ (“humidity, moisture, wetland, marshland”).

parole.significato: distant ancestor, great-great (mainly used in compound words such as ükapa (“great-great-grandfather”))
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *ewkkɜ (“old woman; grandmother”). Cognates include Finnish eukko.

parole.significato: to hit, strike, beat, knock, slap, smack
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Proto-Finno-Ugric *äktä- (“hit, beat, cut”). Cognate with Komi-Zyrian йӧктыны (jöktyny).

parole.significato: he, she (third-person singular, nominative form; usually omitted as redundant due to the verb suffix, except for emphas…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *sᴕ̈ (“he, she, it”). Cognates include Southern Mansi tü, tüw-, Northern Mansi тав (tav, “he, she”), Finnish hän.
From Proto-Finno-Ugric *säwnä (“sp. of fish”). Compare also Finnish säyne, säynäs, Estonian säinas, Northern Sami seavnnját and Kildin Sami сивн (sivn).

From Proto-Finno-Ugric *sükśe. Cognates include Southern Mansi tüks, Northern Mansi таквс (takvs, “autumn”), Udmurt сӥзьыл (siźyl), Moksha сёксе (śokse), Erzya сёксь (śokś), Finnish syksy, Estonian sügis.

Two options: * either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćolme (“knot, bundel; to bind”), cf. Hungarian csomó (“knot”), for the semantic shift cf. also German Knoten (“knot”) vs. Knochen (“bone”) (with a noun-forming suffix -t added in Hungarian, cf. evet, nyest, menyét, but the last three words might have a d

Probably a compound word. The first element is related to the base word of emse (“sow”) (originally meant “female”), which in turn is from Proto-Uralic *emä (“mother, woman”). The second element is either a variant of férj (“husband”) which originally meant “man” or is related to an unattested stem
According to Aikio (2016), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kodwa (“short time, while”). Alternatively, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kalɜ- (“to spend a night”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: leaf (thin, flattened organ of most vegetative plants)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Either derived from the same supposed stem as lebeg (“to float”); or from Proto-Ugric or perhaps Proto-Finno-Ugric *lᴕ̈pɜ, *lepɜ (“leaf”) (compare Erzya лопа (lopa, “leaf”)). The meaning “letter” is attested from the 14th century onwards.

Of debated origin. Either: # Borrowed from Alanic. Compare Ossetian марг (marg, “poison”). Further akin to Persian مرگ (marg, “death”). # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mirkkɜ (“poison”). Compare Finnish myrkky (“poison”), but this is problematic.

parole.significato: to skin (especially an animal) (to remove the skin and/or fur of)
parole.testo: The stem is of disputed origin: either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńowe- (“to skin, flay”) (compare Proto-Samic *ńuovëtēk (“to skin”)) or from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńujɜ- (“to skin, flay”) (compare Udmurt [Term?] (“to skin”), Southern Mansi њо̄йөӈ (ńōjôň, “to skin”)). Uncertain. * Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *śeppä (“skilled”) through Proto-Ugric *seppä. Hence also Proto-Samic *čeappē (“skillful”) and Proto-Finnic *seppä (“smith”). This explanation faces semantic difficulties. * Alternatively from a Turkic language, whence Chuvash шеп (šep, “beautiful”).

parole.significato: to determine the direction in which someone or something proceeds
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wetä-. Cognates include Finnish vetää. The Finno-Ugric root may be related to Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ-, either as loan or through genetic relationship.

From the same root as vezet (“to lead; drive”) + -ér (noun-forming suffix). The root is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wetä- (“to lead, guide, draw, pull”). Cognates include Finnish vetää. parole.significato: branch (the woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing)
parole.testo: Of disputed origin. Either: * From Proto-Ugric *ϑaŋɜ (“branch, twig”). Cognates include Northern Mansi таг (tag, “twig, branch”). * From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šaŋka. Cognates include Finnish hanka.

parole.significato: to soak, steep (to be saturated with liquid by being immersed in it)
parole.testo: Of debated origin. Either from Proto-Ugric *ϑᴕćɜ- (“to become damp, get wet”) or from Proto-Finno-Ugric *sᴕsɜ- (“to become wet”) + -ik.
First attested in c. 1490. Of debated origin. Either from Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic *wᴕlmɜ (“lead”).

Of debated origin. Either from a Proto-Finno-Ugric stem + -öm (noun-forming suffix), or derived from a stem of Turkic origin, the same as in örül (“to be happy, rejoice”) and örvend (“to have pleasure, enjoy”).
